messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Rohan is a 41-year-old South Asian architect, married, who presented for psychological assessment following a period of sustained physical abuse perpetrated by a previous long-term romantic partner. Although that relationship ended several years ago, Rohan describes his daily life as one of barely managed dread, and his PCL-5 score of 70 places him in the severe range of PTSD symptomatology.

The abuse occurred across approximately two years of that earlier relationship. His partner would drink heavily and, when intoxicated, become physically violent — striking him across the face and chest, screaming in a way that dissolved into incoherent noise, her words blurring into sounds he could not parse or predict. On the worst nights, Rohan had been unwell with a winter illness when she attacked him; the combination of his physical vulnerability and her sudden escalation had left him unable to defend himself or even fully process what was happening. He remembered lying on the floor of their apartment, feverish and disoriented, the smell of alcohol sharp in the cold air, the sound of her voice a wall of unintelligible sound. He had not fought back. He had not left. He had not told anyone. He had, he now believed, failed every test a man could fail.

The memories do not arrive as narrative. Rohan describes them as a series of photographs — a close-up of her raised hand, the grain of the floorboards against his cheek, the amber blur of a whiskey glass — each image vivid and dimensionless, stripped of context but saturated with the original terror. When these images surface, they do not feel like recollection; they feel like re-entry. The fear he experiences in those moments is physiologically identical to the fear he felt on the floor of that apartment, and in the wake of each intrusion, the conviction returns with renewed force: he had been betrayed by the one person whose trust he had built his life around, and he had done nothing. This belief — that he is a man who cannot be counted on to act — has become load-bearing in his psychology, and each time the memories erupt with their full original terror, they seem to him to confirm it. He had failed in his most important role. He cannot trust himself to do the right thing.

What makes Rohan's daily life so difficult is that the triggers are everywhere and ordinary. At his architecture firm, a colleague who speaks quickly and excitedly across an open-plan office sometimes produces a wash of overlapping voices that, for a moment, becomes incomprehensible — and in that moment, Rohan's body responds before his mind has caught up. His heart rate surges, his hands go cold, and he is already scanning the room for threat before he has consciously registered what alarmed him. The smell of alcohol at a client dinner, or the faint nausea of a seasonal cold, produces the same pre-conscious mobilisation. These sensory encounters do not merely startle him — they pull the photographs forward, flooding him with the specific images and the specific terror of those nights, and with them comes the familiar weight of self-reproach: he should have seen it coming, he should have acted differently, he was betrayed because he allowed himself to be. The heightened state of alert that follows these episodes persists long into the evening, and by night he cannot surrender to sleep because some part of him remains convinced that vigilance is the only protection he has left.

This vigilance, in turn, keeps the system running. The sustained arousal means that smaller and smaller cues register as potential danger, which means that the triggers multiply, which means that the intrusive photographs come more frequently, which means the appraisals of failure and betrayal are reinforced with greater regularity. His wife has noticed that he flinches when she raises her voice in laughter. He has declined two client hospitality events this year, citing workload. He has not explained any of this to her.

What finally brought Rohan to seek help was a morning when he became mildly ill with a stomach complaint and spent the entire workday unable to concentrate, certain that something terrible was about to happen. He arrived home, sat down at the kitchen table, and could not stand up for an hour. He is most afraid that the person he has become is the person he has always been. He hopes, with some difficulty, that this is not true.
